You put actions in order with prima di + infinitive, dopo aver / essere + participle, appena and finché, to describe a house move and make a plan.
Before bringing the furniture, we'll paint.
As soon as Gennaro arrives, we'll start.
To use prima di + infinitive: Prima di partire, chiamami.
To form the past infinitive: aver fatto, essere arrivato.
To use dopo + past infinitive: Dopo aver mangiato, esco.
To attach pronouns to the infinitive: dopo averlo visto, prima di dirglielo.
To make a step-by-step plan (prima di tutto, poi, infine) and describe a house move.
1st December. Graziella takes Matei and Giulia to the empty flat above the trattoria where she lived with Aldo.
Here's the flat. Before you decide, have a good look at all the rooms.
It's huge! Three rooms, and the kitchen looks onto the garden. Is there a lift too?
No, but it's on the first floor. After climbing four floors on foot for two years, the first floor will feel like a lift to you.
But Graziella, why are you giving it to us? It was your home with Aldo.
Exactly. After standing empty for ten years, this house needs a family. Aldo always used to say: "These rooms are made for children."
I don't know what to say… First of all, thank you.
Thank me after you've painted the walls. Look at that colour: hospital green!
Right, here's the plan: before bringing the furniture, we paint. After painting, we clean. And as soon as everything's dry, we move in.
And Totò? Totò first of all.
Totò comes after the bed, after the wardrobe and after my books. Totò last.
And when are you doing this move?
On the twentieth of December, before Christmas. Gennaro is coming from Naples to help us.
Good. After you've carried up the last box, I'll expect you downstairs in the trattoria for dinner. All of you. Nobody goes to bed until you've eaten.
"dà sul giardino" = looks onto the garden
Stress on "SLO": tra-ZLO-ko, tra-zlo-KA-re. S + L = "zl".
Stress on the FIRST syllable: SKA-to-la. Not "ska-TO-la"!
Stress on "MA": ar-MA-dyo, with "dio" in one syllable.
Stress on the FIRST syllable: STEE-pee-te.
When the subject is the SAME in both parts, "before doing" is PRIMA DI + infinitive:
Before deciding, look at the rooms.
Don't forget "di": "prima DI mangiare", NOT "prima mangiare" and NOT "prima di a mangiare".
With DIFFERENT subjects, use "prima che + subjunctive": "Prima che arrivi Gennaro, puliamo." (Before Gennaro arrives, let's clean.)
"After doing / after having done" is DOPO + the past infinitive: AVER(E) / ESSERE + participle. As in the passato prossimo, verbs with ESSERE make the participle agree:
Dopo essersi svegliata, Giulia ha fatto colazione.
NOT "dopo mangiare" and NOT "dopo che mangiato". You say "dopo AVER mangiato". ("Dopo cena", with a noun, is correct.)
"Avere" usually drops its "-e": "dopo aver finito" sounds more natural than "dopo avere finito".
As with any infinitive, pronouns attach to the end (in the past infinitive, to "aver" / "esser"):
Prima di dirglielo, voglio essere sicura.
Before I tell him, I want to be sure.
Dopo esserci trasferiti, abbiamo fatto una festa.
After moving, we had a party.
The "non" after "finché" isn't a real negative: "finché non arrivi" = "until you arrive". It's optional, but very common.
"Appena" also means "just": "Sono appena arrivato" = "I've just arrived". The context shows the meaning.
To put actions in order, use: prima di tutto (first of all) → poi / dopo (then) → infine / alla fine (finally).
First of all we paint the walls.
Then, after cleaning, we bring in the furniture.
Finally, we put Totò on the balcony.
After arriving, Giulia had a rest.
Per quanto tempo è rimasta vuota?
Di che colore sono le pareti?
Che cosa fanno prima di portare i mobili?

Before starting to paint, Matei studied the walls as if they were a fifteenth-century fresco. He measured everything, did colour tests and wrote a three-page work plan. Giulia read it, laughed and said: "Darling, it's a nursery, not the Sistine Chapel." Then she picked up a roller and started.

They worked every evening for two weeks. After leaving the workshop, they ate a sandwich standing up and went upstairs to paint. Since Giulia mustn't breathe in the paint, Matei did the walls and she chose the colours: pale yellow for the kitchen, light blue for the bedroom and, for the nursery, a warm white, "like Doina's blanket".

One evening, while he was stripping the old wallpaper near the nursery door, Matei stopped. Under the paper, on the wooden door frame, there were little notches made with a knife. Next to each notch was a date written in pencil: 1978, 1979, 1980… up to 1991. And a name, always the same: Marco.

Matei called Giulia, and Giulia went downstairs to fetch Graziella. After seeing the door frame, Graziella sat down on a box and didn't speak for a while. "Aldo made them," she said at last. "Every year, on Marco's birthday. Before cutting the cake, he would stand him against the door and make the notch. Marco always protested, because he wanted to eat straight away."

"When we put up the wallpaper, in 1992, Aldo didn't want to cover them. I insisted, because it seemed childish to me. Then I forgot about them." She touched the highest notch with one finger. "How silly of me. After searching my memory for them for years, they were here, under the paper."

Matei looked at the door frame with a restorer's eye. "Graziella, if you agree, I won't paint over them. I'll clean them and protect them with a clear varnish. And then…" He looked at Giulia, who understood at once. "And then, if you like, we'll carry on. From next year." Graziella didn't answer. She just nodded, her eyes shining with tears.

On the twentieth of December Gennaro arrived, with a van borrowed from a cousin and a tray of Rosaria's lasagne. As soon as he got out of the van, he looked at the stairs of the old building in via della Chiesa and asked: "How many floors?" "Four," said Matei. "No lift." Gennaro crossed himself.

The move lasted from eight in the morning until six in the evening. Marco, who had come specially, helped, and even Radu, Ilinca's boyfriend, who was in Florence for a medical conference and didn't have the courage to say no. Pietro carried the light boxes and shouted "Watch out!" every time someone went past. Signor Franco, sitting on a chair in the street, directed operations the way he used to direct trains.

The problem was the wardrobe. After taking it apart in three pieces, after carrying it down four floors and after loading it into the van, they discovered that it wouldn't go through the door of the new flat. They tried horizontally, vertically, diagonally. Nothing. In the end Gennaro had a Neapolitan idea: the wardrobe went in through the window, hauled up on a rope, while half of via Maggio watched and applauded. The pharmacist came out of his shop to take a photo, and by the evening it was on every phone in the neighbourhood.

At six, after carrying up the last box, they all sat down on the floor in the middle of the living room, exhausted. Giulia looked around: the yellow walls, the boxes, the rescued wardrobe. Then she jumped. "Totò! We've forgotten Totò!" Matei ran all the way to via della Chiesa and came back twenty minutes later, out of breath, with the plant in his arms. Totò, as usual, said nothing.

Before going down to dinner, Giulia took everyone to the nursery door. The door frame was clean and shiny, and Marco's old notches showed up beautifully. Under the last one, from 1991, there was a new notch, very small, almost down by the floor. Beside it, written in pencil: "December. Still in the tummy."

Marco, who was forty-nine, went up to the door frame, touched his notch from when he was eight, then the new one. He turned to his mother. "Dad would be happy," he said. Graziella took his hand. "He is," she replied. "I'm sure of it." Then, before anyone could start crying, she clapped her hands: "To the table! Rosaria's lasagne is getting cold!"
